newsitem.title: USA: U.S. EPA presses for new toxic waste cleanup law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. EPA presses for new toxic waste cleanup law.

text.p: The Clinton administration and Senate Democrats on Tuesday ended any doubt over their position on the Superfund toxic waste cleanup program, saying they wanted to pass a broad bill to overhual the program.

"We continue to believe that a comprehensive reauthorization of the Superfund law is in the best interests of the country," Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Carol Browner said at a news conference.
There had been some doubt about the Democrats' view after Superfund officials said in December that administrative reforms had already speeded up cleanups and cut costs.

Introduction by Senate Democrats last week of narrower legislation to spur redevelopment of abandoned industrial sites, called brownfields, as one of their top 10 bills, also raised doubts about their support for a Superfund bill.
But Sen. Max Baucus of Montana, the top Democrat on the Environment and Public Works Committee, said swift passage of the brownfields bill could help build consensus for a Superfund bill.
"At least if brownfields legislation is passed this year it'll create some momentum for Superfund legislation," he said at a news conference.

Mayor Chris Bollwage of Elizabeth, New Jersey, which is notorious for its wasteland, said passing a brownfields bill was far more important for cities and local communities than Superfund legislation.

"Brownfields (redevelopment) creates jobs," Bollwage said after the news conference. "Superfund legislation, while very, very important, just cleans up environmental contamination," he said, adding that some of the worst toxic waste sites had to be kept out of use for 90 years.
Senate Republicans last week proposed similar measures to encourage brownfields projects, but they were included in a sweeping Superfund reform bill among their top 10 bills.
A Republican aide to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee said brownfields should be addressed in the context of Superfund reform.

Despite their suggestions that gaps between Republicans and Democrats on controversial proposals to change liability and cleanup standards under Superfund were narrowing, the Democrats said a Superfund bill would be tough to pass.
"We have a very good chance to move a brownfields bill expeditiously. I cannot say the same about Superfund," said Sen. Frank Lautenberg, the top Democrat on the Senate Superfund subcommittee.
But Browner and Baucus said that gaps between Republicans and the Democrats would narrow if legislation reflected administrative changes that have been made in the program over the last four years.
